findings.page: PDF p.19 (printed xv) and PDF p.54 (printed 30)
findings.evidence: Preface, PDF p.19: "ANALYTICAL (Axis 3, measurement status) — arithmetic on stated inputs (roofline, KV-residency and capacity screens, the C/W per-host bound (C = per-host KV-slot capacity, W = mean KV-residency time) and the host counts derived from it)".  Ch. 2, PDF p.54: "The symbol is Mweights, not W: throughout the book W is reserved for mean time in system in Little's law, written Lexec = λWexec (Ch 4)."
findings.issue: The symbol W is given two mutually exclusive definitions inside the same book, and the second one (Ch. 2) is the stronger, explicitly book-wide reservation. Ch. 2 asserts W is reserved for 'mean time in system' in Little's law; the Preface's evidence panel assigns W = 'mean KV-residency time' in the C/W per-host capacity bound. Because the C/W bound is the per-host capacity screen that produces every host count in Ch. 16–17, a reader following the Preface would compute with a different W than Ch. 2 sanctions, and cannot tell whether 'KV-residency time' and 'time in system' are meant to be the same quantity (the book elsewhere treats Wexec = 8.58 s as excluding the ~120 ms retrieval term).
findings.fix_instruction: Choose one definition of W and apply it book-wide. Recommended: keep W = mean time in system (Little's law) as Ch. 2 states, and edit the Preface panel to read 'W = mean time in system (Wexec in the canonical scenario)'. If 'mean KV-residency time' is genuinely a distinct quantity, give it its own symbol (e.g. W_res) and state in Ch. 17 how it relates to Wexec. Add one sentence to Ch. 2 §2.3 or Ch. 17 Table 17-1 pinning the identity so the two chapters cannot drift.

findings.evidence: On the canonical 8×H100 host each GPU streams only its 17.5 GB shard — ~21% of peak bandwidth over the 25 ms step — so the binding terms at that operating point are the TP collectives, kernel efficiency, sampling and scheduling, and the ~9.2K-token KV attention read, not the weight read.
findings.issue: The 17.5 GB figure is a per-GPU weight-residency amount, but the prose asserts 'peak bandwidth' without stating that the 80 GB capacity figure is read as decimal 80×10^9 bytes. Without that convention, a reader converting 17.5 GB at 1024^3 per GB gets ~18.8 GB, and the 3.35 TB/s denominator is itself ambiguous (3.35×10^12 B/s). The 21% verdict is arithmetic on 17.5/(3.35e12×0.025)=20.9%, which only holds if 17.5 GB means 17.5e9 bytes AND 3.35 TB/s means 3.35e12 B/s AND the 25 ms step is the exact denominator. The prose does not state the byte-unit convention for HBM capacity or bandwidth here, so the 21% is under-determined.
findings.fix_instruction: State the decimal convention at first use of the 17.5 GB and 3.35 TB/s figures, e.g. '17.5×10^9 B against 3.35×10^12 B/s'.

findings.evidence: decode sits in the memory-bandwidth-bound regime (weight-only arithmetic intensity ≈ 1 FLOP/byte, far left of the roofline ridge)
findings.issue: This is correct per the book's own derivation: 2N FLOPs = 140 GFLOP, N bytes = 140 GB, so 1 FLOP/byte. Confirmed correct.
